title: "Do not despise food. Food is Brahman." (3.7–3.10)
word: "Do not despise food. Food is Br
hook: right after Bhrigu reaches bliss, the Upanishad walks back into the kitchen with four vows about food
tomorrow: the song of one who knows

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman, and is sent away five times. Your line was tapas, go and think. Did you give a question one more round of your own heat? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

You'd expect a story like Bhrigu's to end at the summit. He's found it: bliss is Brahman. Cue the light, roll the credits. Instead, the very next lines of the Taittiriya come straight back down the mountain and into the kitchen. The first thing Bhrigu found, food, the answer that looked too simple, gets the last word. And it's not a vision. It's a set of house rules. Four short vows about eating, sharing and feeding strangers. Today, a very practical page.
screen: `BLISS IS BRAHMAN. ROLL THE CREDITS?` → `NO: BACK TO THE KITCHEN.` → `FOUR VOWS ABOUT FOOD.`

segments.voice: Section seven begins: annam na nindyat, tad vratam. Do not despise food. That is the vow. Then it explains, in pairs. Breath is food, and the body is the eater of food. The body rests on breath, breath rests on the body. Each is food for the other. Section eight: do not reject food. Water is food, and fire is the eater. Section nine: make food plentiful. Earth is food, and space is the eater. Everywhere you look, something is feeding something else, and being held up by it. That's why food is Brahman here. Not a metaphor for something higher. The chain of eating and being eaten is the same chain Bhrigu traced: what beings are born from, live by, and go back into. Anna simply means food, what is eaten. And an earlier verse in the same Upanishad plays on the word: food is eaten by beings, and it eats them in turn, which is why it's called anna. Then section ten puts it into one rule a household can keep. Never turn away anyone who comes asking for a place to stay. So, the text says, gather plenty of food, by whatever means you have. Then you can say to a guest, food is ready. You heard last week, honor the guest as god. Here's the kitchen behind it. In Hindu homes and temples, food is often offered first and received back as prasad, a gift. Some chant a verse of the Gita before meals. Either way, the plate isn't neutral. It's anna.
screen: `DO NOT DESPISE FOOD. THAT IS THE VOW.` · `EVERYTHING EATS AND IS EATEN.` · `ANNA: WHAT IS EATEN.` · `NEVER TURN AWAY A GUEST.` · then, large: `ANNAM BRAHMA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the chain of eating. Sit, and feel a breath come in. The text calls breath food and the body its eater: notice the body taking the breath in. Then notice the body holding the breath, and the breath holding up the body, each resting on the other. Then widen it: the floor holding you up, the air in the room, the light on your skin. Something feeding something else, everywhere you look. Rest inside that chain for a while. The bell holds the time.
Do not despise food. Food is Brahman. The Taittiriya's vow: everything eats and is eaten, so honor the plate, make plenty, and never turn away a guest.
Your line: anna. Today, share some food with someone, or set out a little more than you need, for whoever turns up. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to the deity before eating and receive it back as prasad; feeding guests and the hungry (anna-dana) is counted among the great gifts, and many households and temples serve free meals.

fork.setup: a stranger knocks at night, asking for a place to stay. you weren't expecting anyone. what does the Taittiriya say?
options: send them on; your food is for your family.
never turn them away, so keep plenty of food.
ask them to come back in the morning.
fork.reveal: section ten: never turn away anyone who asks for lodging. so gather plenty of food, and say, food is ready.

original.note: Sanskrit: "do not despise food." the first of four food vows, Taittiriya 3.7.

trapdoor: what you thought: food is fuel; the spiritual stuff is somewhere else.
what it means: food is Brahman: the chain of eating and being eaten that every being is born from, lives by and returns to.
what a scholar hears: four vows in 3.7–3.10: do not despise food, do not reject food, make food plentiful, turn no one away from your home.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.8–3.10 (the food vows; no guest turned away)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.2 (food is eaten and eats beings; hence anna)

notes: Pairs given from memory: 3.7 breath food/body eater; 3.8 water food/fire eater; 3.9 earth food/space eater. Confirm.
3.10: 'na kancana vasatau pratyacakshita, tad vratam' and gathering plenty of food by any means; confirm paraphrase.
2.2 wordplay (adyate 'tti ca bhutani, tasmad annam tad ucyate) paraphrased; confirm placement.
Mealtime Gita verse (commonly 4.24, brahmarpanam) mentioned without naming; widely practiced but not universal.
'You heard last week, honor the guest as god' refers to day 390 (1.11).
